680.title: Pray for one another (James 5:13–20)
680.hook: sick? call the elders; suffering? pray; cheerful? sing
680.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament based in part on James 5:14–15, and many Protestant churches have elders or ministers anoint and pray over the sick; most churches also pray for the sick by name in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the patient farmer, and your line was be patient. What did you do within reach instead of pushing on what you were waiting for? Day six hundred eighty.

Some letters end with a long goodbye. James doesn't. No greetings, no names, no farewell. His last paragraph reads like a quick list on the fridge before a long trip: if this happens, do this. If that happens, do that. Sad? Happy? Sick? Wandering? There's an instruction for each. And almost every one of them points to the same thing. Not a technique. Not a rule. Other people, and prayer. The last word of a blunt, practical letter turns out to be about how a community holds each other up.

In the King James Bible: "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms." Every mood has a place to go. Hard days, bring them to God. Good days, sing. Then: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves. The sick person calls, and the elders come. They come to the bedside. Oil was a common medicine in the ancient world, and also a sign of being set apart for God. Churches practice this verse differently. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, it's one of the roots of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestant churches also anoint and pray over the sick, as a practice of prayer rather than a sacrament. Then: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." One to another. Not only up to God, but sideways, to each other. And the example James chooses is encouraging. Elijah, he says, was a man subject to like passions as we are. An ordinary human, moody, tired, frightened at times. He prayed, and rain was held back, and he prayed again, and it came. James's point isn't that you need to be a giant. It's that ordinary people's prayers matter. The very last line: whoever brings back someone who has wandered from the truth saves a soul and covers a multitude of sins. The letter ends not with a farewell, but with someone going after someone else.

Here's the practice: pray for one sick person, or hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is ill right now. A friend, a parent, a coworker, a child, someone you've only heard about. Picture them as clearly as you can: where they are, what the room looks like, what they might be feeling. Don't rush. Then, if you pray, pray for them by name, in your own words, as James says, one for another. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention with care, and wish them well. Then think of one way to let them know. The bell holds the time.
Pray for one another. James's last instruction: bring every mood to God, call others to the bedside, and hold one another up.
Your line: pray for one another. Today, send the sick person you thought of a short message, so they know someone is holding them in mind. Day six hundred eighty.

681.title: What we have touched (1 John 1:1–4)
681.hook: the elder writes of what he has seen, heard and touched
681.howItsDone: Some churches read 1 John 1:1–4 in the Christmas season, as a witness that the Word became flesh, and use the letter's opening when teaching about fellowship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of James, and your line was pray for one another. Did you send that message to someone who's sick? Day six hundred eighty-one.

You can read a whole biography of someone. Dates, places, letters, photographs. And still not know the feel of their handshake, or how their voice sounded saying a name. Some knowing goes through the eyes and ears, and some goes through the skin. Today a new letter opens, called First John. It has no greeting, no name, no to-whom. It starts mid-breath, like a witness on the stand who can't wait to say what he knows. And the first thing he talks about is touch.

In the King James Bible: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life." Listen to the senses pile up. Heard. Seen. Looked upon, a word for gazing, taking it in. And then, handled. Touched. The word means to feel for something, the way you might reach out in the dark. From the beginning echoes the first line of John's Gospel: in the beginning was the Word. For this writer, the Word of life is someone you could touch. Who's writing? The letter never says. Tradition says John the apostle, and the style is close to John's Gospel. Some scholars think it comes from a community shaped by that Gospel, and hear the same voice as the one who calls himself the elder in Second and Third John. Either way, the voice speaks as a witness: we were there, we saw, we touched. And why does he say it this way? Because some people, it seems, were teaching that Jesus only seemed to have a real body. A spirit wearing a costume. The writer answers with his own hands. We touched him, he says. He was real flesh. Then the purpose: "That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us." Fellowship is a deep word: sharing, partnership, a common life. Not a club. And then the last line of the opening, the reason he's writing at all: "And these things write we unto you, that your joy may be full." He doesn't write to win an argument. He writes so the joy can be full.

Here's the practice: touch something real and give thanks. Settle, and breathe. Put your hand on something near you. The table. Your own arm. A cup. The floor under your feet. Feel it fully: the temperature, the texture, the weight. Notice that you don't have to believe it's there. You know it through your hand. Stay with that for a while. Then, slowly, let your mind move to one person whose hand you've held, and remember the feel of it. If you pray, you can give thanks for what is real and near. The bell holds the time.
What we have touched. First John's opening: the Word of life, heard, seen and handled, a witness to real flesh, so that joy may be full.
Your line: what we have touched. Today, give one real hug, handshake or hand on a shoulder to someone you love, and let it last a second longer than usual. Day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: God is light (1 John 1:5–10)
682.hook: if we confess, he is faithful to forgive
682.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess sins to God in the presence of a priest in the sacrament of confession; some Protestant services include a spoken prayer of confession, sometimes introduced with 1 John 1:8–9, followed by words of forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of First John, and your line was what we have touched. Whose hand or shoulder did you hold a second longer? Day six hundred eighty-two.

Walk into a dark room and flip on the light. The first thing you see is not the furniture. It's the mess. The clothes on the chair. The dust on the shelf. The mug you forgot about. In the dark, the room seemed fine. In the light, it's honest. That's why some of us prefer dim lighting. Today's passage starts with a statement about God that is three words long in English. And then it moves, straight away, to what happens to our mess when that light comes on.

In the King James Bible: "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." No shadows in the corners. Nothing hidden, nothing half-true. Then the writer draws the conclusion: if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. Light isn't only about God. It's about honesty between people. And then a run of ifs, like doors. Watch the traps. If we say we have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, we lie. And: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." The danger isn't having a mess. The letter takes for granted that there is one. The danger is saying there isn't one. Then the open door: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." The Greek word for confess is built from same and say: to say the same thing, to agree. To confess is to finally say about your life what God already says about it, what the light already shows. No more spin. And the response isn't a lecture. It's two words: faithful and just. Faithful, because God keeps his promise to forgive. Just, because the letter has just said that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin. Churches practice confession differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to God in the presence of a priest, in the sacrament of confession or reconciliation. Many Protestants confess privately to God, or together in a prayer of confession during worship, and some confess to a trusted friend. Each takes this verse to heart in its own way.
screen: `CONFESS: SAY THE SAME AS THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: confess one thing. Settle, and breathe. Picture a lamp coming on in a room inside you. Let it shine on one thing you've done, or not done, that you've been avoiding looking at. Not your whole life. One thing. Name it plainly to yourself, without excuses and without beating yourself up. Just say the same thing the light says. If you pray, you can say it to God, and then rest in the words faithful and just to forgive. If you don't, sit for a moment in the relief of not pretending. The bell holds the time.
Confession. Saying the same thing about your life that the light already shows, and finding God faithful to forgive.
Your line: faithful to forgive. Today, if you owe someone an apology, say it plainly, with no but on the end. Day six hundred eighty-two.

683.title: The old new commandment (1 John 2:1–11)
683.hook: whoever hates his brother walks in darkness
683.howItsDone: Christians remember the new commandment especially on Maundy Thursday, whose name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, commandment, and many churches read 1 John 2 when teaching about love within the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God is light, and the word confession. Your line was faithful to forgive. Did you manage an apology with no but on the end? Day six hundred eighty-three.

Is it old or new? The writer of First John can't seem to decide, and that's the point. In the space of two verses he says, I'm not writing you a new commandment, it's an old one. And then, right away: actually, it is a new commandment. It sounds like a man changing his mind halfway through a sentence. It isn't. Ask a couple married for decades. The same words, I love you, can be very old and brand new at once. Today, the commandment that is both.

He starts tenderly: "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." An advocate is someone who stands beside you in court and speaks for you. Then he gives a simple test: how do we know we know God? We keep his commandments. Not just say we do. Then the riddle. "Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning." Which old commandment? Love. It runs back through the Torah: "love thy neighbour as thyself," in Leviticus. It's what his readers heard from the very beginning of their faith. And then he flips it: "Again, a new commandment I write unto you." New, because in John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, Jesus says, "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another." New, because now it has a face: love as he loved. And new, the writer says, "because the darkness is past, and the true light now shineth." It's dawn. Something old is being seen in fresh light. Then the hard edge: "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now." You can't claim to be in the light and hate the person next to you. And here's the image: whoever hates walks in darkness and doesn't know where he's going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes. Hatred doesn't only hurt the other person. It takes away your own sight. Love is how you see where you're going.
screen: then, large: `THE TRUE LIGHT NOW SHINETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace with one person, starting inside. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you hold something against. It might be small, an irritation, or big, an old hurt. Picture them. Notice what happens in your chest. Now notice the line in the letter: darkness blinds the one who hates. Ask: what has this grudge kept me from seeing? About them, about me, about the way forward? You don't have to fix it in two minutes. Just take one step toward peace in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The old new commandment. Love one another: old as the Torah, new in Christ's love, seen fresh as the true light shines.
Your line: walk in the light. Today, take one real step toward peace with someone: a message, a kind word, or simply dropping a story you keep retelling about them. Day six hundred eighty-three.

684.title: Little children (1 John 2:12–17)
684.hook: the elder writes tenderly to children, young people and elders
684.howItsDone: Some churches read 1 John 2:12–14 as a blessing for every age in a congregation, and the warning about the lust of the eyes and the pride of life comes up in teaching on simple living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old new commandment, and your line was walk in the light. What step did you take toward peace with someone? Day six hundred eighty-four.

Families have pet names. Kiddo. Sweetheart. Buddy. Some grandparents call grown adults by a childhood nickname until the end, and nobody minds, because it isn't about age. It's about belonging. The writer of First John has a pet name for his readers, and he keeps coming back to it: little children. In today's passage, he stops the flow of the letter and writes a little poem, a set of short lines addressed to everyone in the room, young and old. And then a warning about what can pull them away.

In the King James Bible: "I write unto you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one." And then he goes round the circle again: children, fathers, young men. Little children: you're forgiven. Fathers, the older ones: you have known him a long time. Young people: you are strong, the word of God lives in you, and you've already won a battle. Scholars aren't sure whether he means actual ages, or stages of faith, or whether all three are said to everyone at once. Maybe all three. On that reading, every reader is a little child who is forgiven, a mature one who knows, and a young one who is strong. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't write to scold. Every line turns on the word because: because you're forgiven, because you know, because you've overcome. He writes from what's already true of them. Then the warning: "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world." That can sound strange next to John's Gospel, where God so loved the world. But world here seems to mean something different: the way of life that leaves God out. He names it: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life." Wanting, looking, showing off. Appetite, envy, status. And he puts it in perspective: "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever." Trends pass. The one who does the will of God abides.
screen: then, large: `I WRITE UNTO YOU, LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a tender note, in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone younger than you, a child, a student, a new coworker, a younger sibling. Then someone older, a parent, a mentor, a neighbor. Then someone in the middle, a friend your own age. For each one, finish this sentence in your head: I'm writing to you because. Because you're forgiven. Because you've taught me. Because you're strong. Don't write what they should do. Write what's already true of them. If you pray, you can pray for each by name. The bell holds the time.
Little children. The writer's pet name for his readers: forgiven, belonging, written to because of what's already true.
Your line: little children. Today, send one of those three people a short note that begins, I'm writing because, and finish it with something true and kind. Day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: What manner of love (1 John 3:1–3)
685.hook: see what love: that we should be called children of God
685.howItsDone: Many Christians read 1 John 3:1–2 at baptisms and on All Saints' Day, and the line about seeing God as he is shapes Christian hope in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elder's pet name, and your line was little children. Who got your note that began, I'm writing because? Day six hundred eighty-five.

Somewhere in a lot of families there's a box. Inside: crayon drawings, a first shoe, a report card, a lock of hair. Plenty of people only find it as adults, clearing out a closet, and it stops them cold: someone kept all of this, because it was mine. A love they never saw, kept the whole time. Today's passage is only three verses long, and it begins with that kind of surprise. The writer of First John has been talking about light and darkness, sin and commandments. Then he stops, as if he's suddenly overcome, and says: look.

In the King James Bible: "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God." Behold. Look at this. What manner of love: the Greek phrase carries surprise, something like, what kind of love is this? Where does love like this even come from? Bestowed is a gift word. Not earned. Given. And the gift is a name: called children of God. Here's a detail from the manuscripts. The oldest Greek manuscripts add three more words after that line, and so we are. Called children of God, and so we are. The manuscripts behind the King James didn't have those words, and modern translations usually put them back. It's as if the writer heard the word called and worried someone would think it was only a title. It isn't only a title. It's what you are. Then he adds why the world doesn't always see it: "therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not." If people missed who Jesus was, they'll miss who his children are too. Then the future, and here he admits what he doesn't know: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." Now. Already. But not yet finished. We don't know what we'll be. What we do know, he says, is that when he appears, "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is." And the last verse says hope like that changes how you live now: whoever has this hope purifies himself.
screen: `BEHOLD: WHAT KIND OF LOVE IS THIS?`
`NOW, BUT NOT YET WHAT WE SHALL BE.`
`WE SHALL SEE HIM AS HE IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear a kinder name. Settle, and breathe. Think of the names you call yourself in a hard moment. Failure. Idiot. Too much. Not enough. Notice them without arguing. Then, slowly, set beside them the name the letter uses: children of God. If you pray, you can hear it with your own name in front of it. If that phrase isn't yours, try a plainer one: I am loved. Notice what happens in your body. Rest there, and just look. The bell holds the time.
What manner of love. The wonder of First John: love so surprising that we're called children of God, and so we are.
Your line: children of god. Today, each time you hear yourself use a harsh name for yourself, notice it, and set a kinder one beside it. Day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: In deed and in truth (1 John 3:11–18)
686.hook: love not in word only but in deed
686.howItsDone: Christians organizing meal trains, collections and visiting sometimes quote 1 John 3:18, and churches read it alongside James 2 on faith and works.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what manner of love, and your line was children of god. Which harsh name for yourself did you swap out? Day six hundred eighty-six.

A heart emoji takes half a second. A sympathy post takes ten. Driving across town with soup takes an afternoon. All three can be sincere. But only one of them is warm when it arrives. For days now, First John has circled love: old, new, the love that names believers children of God. Today he gets very practical. He reaches back to Cain and Abel, and then he asks a question about a bank account and a neighbor in need. Here a letter that can sometimes float comes down to earth.

In the King James Bible: "For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another." Then the counterexample, from the first pages of Genesis: don't be like Cain, who killed his brother. The writer goes further: whoever hates his brother is a murderer at heart. Hatred is the seed; Cain shows what it grows into. So what does love look like? Not a feeling first. A shape. "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." For Christians, the cross is the measure of love. And then, right away, the writer brings it down from the heroic to the everyday. Laying down a life is rare. But: "whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?" Bowels of compassion sounds odd to us. The Greek word means the inner organs, the gut, where feeling was felt. We still say a gut feeling, or it hit me in the stomach. The picture is of someone who sees a need, feels that tug inside, and shuts it off. Then the line this whole passage builds to: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." In deed: something done. In truth: something real, not a performance. This week we've walked from the end of James into First John: pray for one another, what we have touched, God is light, the old new commandment, little children, what manner of love, and now, in deed and in truth.
screen: `HE LAID DOWN HIS LIFE FOR US.`
then, large: `IN DEED AND IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one loving deed. Settle, and breathe. Think of a need you've seen in the last week that tugged at you. Someone tired, someone short of money, someone lonely, someone sick. Remember the tug, the gut feeling. Notice if you shut it off, and why: busy, unsure, embarrassed. No blame. Now choose one small deed you could actually do about it. Not a feeling. Not a post. A deed. Picture yourself doing it, step by step, until you can see it clearly. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to follow through. The bell holds the time.
In deed and in truth. Love that does something real, not only words or the tongue: an open hand to a brother or sister in need.
screen: `IN DEED AND IN TRUTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not in word only. Today, do the deed you pictured, even a small version of it, before you post or say anything about it. Day six hundred eighty-six.

seeing a brother in need and not shutting up compassion.

fork.setup: you have plenty, and you see a friend in real need. you feel the tug. what does the letter ask?
options: send warm words and move on.
open your hand and help, in deed and in truth.
wait until they ask.
fork.reveal: "how dwelleth the love of God in him?" the writer asks of anyone who shuts up compassion. "let us not love in word... but in deed and in truth."

original.note: Greek: inner organs, the gut, and so compassion. the KJV renders it bowels of compassion.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to people.
what it means: love measured by a laid-down life, and brought down to an open hand for a neighbor in need.
what a scholar hears: splanchna, the gut as the seat of feeling, and Cain as the dark counterpoint to love from the beginning.
